title: The Lost Sheep, the Lost Coin, and the Lost Sons

verses.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus.
So the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."
Then Jesus told them this parable:
"What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?
And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders,
comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!'
I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.
Or what woman who has ten silver coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it?
And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors to say, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.'
In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God's angels over one sinner who repents."
Then Jesus said, "There was a man who had two sons.
The younger son said to him, 'Father, give me my share of the estate.' So he divided his property between them.
After a few days, the younger son got everything together and journeyed to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth in wild living.
After he had spent all he had, a severe famine swept through that country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed the pigs.
He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, but no one would give him a thing.
Finally he came to his senses and said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have plenty of food, but here I am, starving to death!
I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.'"
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
The son declared, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.'
But the father said to his servants, 'Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!' So they began to celebrate.
Meanwhile the older son was in the field, and as he approached the house, he heard music and dancing.
So he called one of the servants and asked what was going on.
'Your brother has returned,' he said, 'and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has him back safe and sound.'
The older son became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and pleaded with him.
But he answered his father, 'Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!'
'Son, you are always with me,' the father said, 'and all that is mine is yours.
But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.'"

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Three linked parables told in answer to a complaint, sometimes called the Gospel within the Gospel
context.audience: Two groups at once: tax collectors and sinners who have gathered to listen, and Pharisees and scribes who grumble about it. The parables are aimed at the second group and welcome the first.
context.setting: Jesus is still traveling toward Jerusalem and is surrounded by people whom respectable society kept at a distance. Sharing a meal meant fellowship, so "eats with them" (v.2) is the real complaint. Sheep, coins, and family estates were everyday realities for the listeners, and the pig-feeding job of the younger son (v.15) would have horrified a Jewish audience, since pigs were unclean.
context.custom: A father did not normally divide his estate while alive, and for a son to ask for his share (v.12) was to wish him dead in effect. A dignified older man did not run, so the father's sprint to meet his son (v.20) breaks the social rules. The best robe, a ring, and sandals (v.22) were signs of full sonship, since hired servants and slaves were often barefoot. A "fattened calf" meant a feast for the whole village.
context.timelineImmediate: Luke 14 ended with the cost of following Jesus and the warning about salt that loses its taste. Chapter 15 shows the other side: the joy of the God who seeks and welcomes the lost. Luke 16 will turn to the use of money and the rich man and Lazarus, and speak again to the Pharisees.
context.timelineBible: The shepherd image recalls Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's leaders for neglecting the flock and promises to seek the lost sheep Himself. The father's compassion echoes Hosea 11 and Jeremiah 31:20, where God calls Israel His son and longs for him. The younger son who ends up with pigs also echoes Joseph and Jonah, who both went down before being brought up.
context.sparkNotes: The Pharisees grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners, so He answers with three stories about something lost and found: a sheep, a coin, and a son. In each, the one who finds it throws a party, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. The third story has two sons. The younger one wastes his inheritance, comes to his senses among the pigs, and is met on the road and welcomed by his running father. The older son is angry and will not go in, and the story ends with the father pleading with him, without telling us whether he does.

translation.meaning: To receive someone gladly and take them in, here with the sense of table fellowship. The Pharisees mean it as an accusation, but it is the best summary of Jesus' ministry.
To change one's mind and turn. In the lost sheep and coin the object does nothing, which shows that repentance here is the sinner's response to being found, and is itself a cause of joy.
Literally "coming to himself." The phrase describes sinful life as a kind of madness, and the turn home begins with seeing things as they are.
A strong word from splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. It is the same verb used for the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:33 and for Jesus at Nain in Luke 7:13.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's version of the lost sheep, told to the disciples about not despising little ones.

otBackground.note: God promises to search for His scattered sheep and bring them back, the background for the shepherd who goes after the one.
The Lord as shepherd who leads and restores, the picture behind the shepherd carrying the sheep home.
God as a father whose compassion will not let Israel go, even after rebellion.
Ephraim, God's dear son, whom He still remembers and for whom His heart yearns.
"We all, like sheep, have gone astray," which lies beneath the whole chapter.

commentary.note: Henry reads the lost sheep as a sinner lost to God, to the flock, and to himself, and notes that "God follows backsliding sinners with the calls of his word and the strivings of his Spirit." Of the coin he says "the soul is silver, of intrinsic worth and value," even when it has fallen into the dirt. In both stories the joy is the point: heaven's response to one sinner who repents is celebration, which is exactly what the Pharisees could not share.

On the prodigal son Henry reads the far country as the world, where sinners take up residence, and notes that "he came to himself" means he had been out of his mind, since sin is "a state of madness and frenzy." On the father running, he writes: "Here were feet of mercy, and those feet quick-paced." On the older brother, he says that those who are "comparatively innocents seldom know how to be compassionate towards those who are manifestly penitents."

Gill reads the ninety-nine "just persons, which need no repentance" as the scribes and Pharisees who thought themselves righteous, and he insists that real repentance includes faith in Christ and a true leaving of sin. On the coin, he takes the woman as Christ, the lamp as the Gospel, and the sweeping as its preaching. On "came to himself" he says an unregenerate person is "beside himself." He reads the robe as the imputed righteousness of Christ, the ring as God's everlasting love, and the shoes as a walk shaped by the gospel of peace.

overview.summary: The Pharisees grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners, so He tells of a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. In each, the finder throws a party. The younger son is welcomed home by a running father, while the older brother stays outside.
overview.settingLine: Tax collectors and sinners gathered around Jesus.

history.t: Respectable society kept tax collectors and notorious sinners at a distance.
Many Jews lived across the Mediterranean, so a son might wander far into foreign lands.

customs.t: A father rarely divided his estate while alive, so the younger son's request was an insult.
Dignified older men didn't run, so the father's sprint broke every social rule.

archaeology.t: Silver drachmas like the lost coin were worth about a day's wage.
Stone sheepfolds still dot the Judean hills, where flocks spent the night.

overview.discussion: The older brother did everything right, yet felt shut out. Why does Jesus leave his ending open?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
overview.author: Luke
overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
